A literature review is a codable sequence of steps, not a genre of writing. Version the recipe — extraction rules, validation gates, synthesis prompts — in git. Run it, get an essay. input.file_text:
---
title: zettel as cross-source idea graph
date: 2026-05-26
type: zet
status: draft
project: zettel
tools: GitHub, Claude
tags: zettel, literature-review, knowledge-graph, doi, bidirectional-indexing, lazy-bibliography
source: claude-conversation
capture_mode: live
model: claude-sonnet-4-6
decisions_made:
  - Each zettel is an idea tagged to multiple sources via DOI — not one source per zettel
  - Inversion of typical annotation: sources serve ideas, not ideas serving sources
  - Bidirectional indexing from day one: zettels → sources (via DOI tags), sources → zettels (via index query)
  - Bibliography metadata is lazy-loaded only at citation time — no point maintaining it for sources you may never cite
  - At citation time, query "show me all zettels tagged with DOI X" to assemble both bibliography and argument simultaneously
open_questions:
  - How do you handle a zettel whose idea spans sources from incompatible disciplinary frameworks?
  - What's the minimum DOI tagging discipline needed before the graph becomes queryable?
next_actions:
  - Define zettel YAML field for source handles (doi:, isbn:, url:, arxiv:) in zet skill update
linked_notes:
  - 2026-05-26-doi-citation-dna
  - 2026-05-26-litreview-runnable-process
  - tools/skills/zet.md
---

In a literature review zettelkasten, each zettel captures an idea that appears across multiple sources, tagged to those sources via DOI or equivalent handle. This inverts standard annotation (one note per paper) in favor of one note per idea, tagged to all papers where it appears. The graph is bidirectional from day one: zettels reference sources via handles; sources can be queried to return all zettels that cite them. Bibliography metadata — author, title, journal, date — is never maintained speculatively. It is fetched on demand at the moment of citation, only for sources that made it into the argument. This keeps the pipeline light, the notes portable, and the graph clean. The DOI is sufficient as a citation anchor; full metadata is a presentation layer, not a knowledge layer.

date: 2026-05-26

  - DOI is the primary persistent handle for published journal articles and many books
  - ISBN is the fallback for books without DOIs

  - Institutional repository handles cover theses and local documents
  - Zotero is an optional browse/collection layer, not a required pipeline component — dissolvable
  - The DOI is the path to the PDF; storing the PDF locally is optional, not required
  - Handle hierarchy: DOI → ISBN → URL (Wayback-archived) → institutional repo link

  - Should arXiv IDs get their own field or fall under URL?

linked_notes:

  - 2026-05-26-litreview-runnable-process
---

The DOI (Digital Object Identifier) functions as citation DNA in a markdown-native literature review pipeline: persistent, resolvable, sufficient to reconstruct the source at any future point. The handle hierarchy for sources without DOIs: ISBN (books), then URL with a Wayback Machine archived snapshot as a durability layer, then institutional repository link (theses, local reports). Zotero remains useful as a collection and browsing interface during the search phase but is not a required pipeline component — a shared Zotero export in git (one file per contributor, version-controlled) can serve the same function without introducing dependency. The PDF is recoverable from the DOI at any time; local storage is optional. This keeps the pipeline lightweight: the zettel carries the handle, the handle gets you the source, full metadata is generated on demand.

input.file_text:
---
title: validation gates in zettel extraction
date: 2026-05-26
type: zet
status: draft
project: zettel
tools: Claude, GitHub
tags: zettel, literature-review, quality-gates, validation, human-in-loop, knowledge-graph
source: claude-conversation
capture_mode: live
model: claude-sonnet-4-6
decisions_made:
  - Zettel quality must be monitored as the source graph grows — sprawl and drift are the primary failure modes
  - At 5+ sources: trigger a machine check — "Do all these sources actually support the same claim, or did the model conflate them?"
  - At 20+ sources: trigger human validation — zettel has reached synthesis/publication threshold
  - Loops can be machine or human depending on cost and consequence
  - The check itself is a queryable operation: re-prompt the model with zettel claim + all tagged sources
open_questions:
  - What constitutes a coherent zettel at the machine-check stage — cosine similarity? Re-extraction agreement?
  - Who triggers the 20-source human validation — the contributor, or an automated flag?
  - Should zettels that fail the 5-source check be split, archived, or flagged?
next_actions:
  - Define machine-check prompt for 5-source validation gate
  - Add validation_status field to zettel YAML schema (unvalidated / machine-checked / human-validated)
linked_notes:
  - 2026-05-26-zettel-cross-source-idea-graph
  - 2026-05-26-litreview-runnable-process
---

As a literature review zettelkasten grows, individual zettels accumulate sources that may drift from the original claim — either through model conflation during extraction or through gradual scope creep as spiraling adds tangentially related papers. Two validation gates manage this. At 5+ sources: machine check — re-query the model with the zettel claim and all tagged sources, ask whether they genuinely support the same idea. This catches conflation early. At 20+ sources: human validation required — the zettel has reached a density that implies a finding worth publishing, and a human needs to read a representative sample and write a synthesis argument. Both gates produce a validation_status field in zettel YAML: unvalidated, machine-checked, human-validated. The pipeline is self-auditing by design.

---
title: Literature Review Workflow
date: 2026-05-26
version: v1
type: artifact
artifact_type: methods-doc
project: zettel
slug: literature-review-workflow
status: draft
tags: zettel, literature-review, pipeline, zotero, doi, pdf-to-text, zettelkasten, ai-rtw
source: claude-conversation

# Literature Review Workflow

A repeatable, AI-assisted pipeline for PhD-scale literature reviews. Markdown-native, version-controlled, cross-disciplinary. The pipeline produces a set of idea-based zettel notes tagged to source identifiers — not an annotated bibliography. The essay emerges from the zettel graph.

---

## Stage 1 — Search and Collect

**Goal:** Build a Zotero collection of 30–50 candidate sources.

1. Search library databases (JSTOR, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, disciplinary databases as appropriate) using your research question as the anchor.
2. As you find sources that look promising — title catches your attention, abstract suggests relevance — save them to your shared Zotero library via the **Zotero browser connector with institutional proxy active**.
   - The proxy ensures PDFs are captured automatically where your library has access.
   - Do not curate at this stage. Collect broadly. You want 50–80 candidates before narrowing.
3. All contributors save to the **same shared Zotero group library** for this project.
4. The Zotero library file is committed to the shared GitHub repository so it is version-controlled and accessible to all collaborators and to the model.

---

## Stage 2 — Abstract Screen and Tag

**Goal:** Narrow the collection to 30–50 sources worth pursuing. Tag them for pipeline entry.

1. Read the abstract of each saved source. If it looks genuinely relevant to your research question, **tag it `aaa` in Zotero**.
   - `aaa` sorts to the top of the tag list alphabetically — easy to filter and select.
   - This tag means: "I have read the abstract and this source is worth full processing."
   - Sources without `aaa` stay in the library but are not processed further unless you return to them.
2. Aim for 30–50 `aaa`-tagged sources. Fewer than 30 may indicate the search was too narrow; more than 50 makes the next stages expensive.
3. For sources where the abstract is insufficient to judge relevance, skim the introduction and conclusion before deciding.

---

## Stage 3 — Export from Zotero

**Goal:** Produce a BIB file and a set of PDFs for pipeline processing.

1. In Zotero, filter by tag `aaa` to show only your screened sources.
2. Select all filtered sources.
3. **Export selected library:** File → Export Library → format: **BibTeX** → save as `sources-aaa.bib` → commit to repo at `[project]/data/sources-aaa.bib`.
4. **Confirm PDFs:** Zotero should have attached PDFs for most sources captured via proxy. For any missing PDFs:
   - Try right-clicking the item → Find Available PDF
   - Or fetch manually via DOI using Unpaywall or your institutional access
   - Note sources with no PDF in a `missing-pdfs.md` file — these will need manual handling in Stage 4

---

## Stage 4 — PDF to Text Conversion

**Goal:** Convert all PDFs to plain text files for model processing.

> **⚠️ Check with Paul Lee before writing this from scratch.** Paul has been working on a PDF-to-text conversion script. Contact him first — his version may already handle batch processing, OCR fallback for scanned PDFs, and filename conventions consistent with the pipeline. If his script is available, use it and document the version here. If not, use the script below as a starting point.

### Interim script (if Paul's is not yet available)

Save as `tools/scripts/pdf_to_text.py` and run from repo root:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
pdf_to_text.py — batch PDF to text conversion for literature review pipeline
Converts all PDFs in an input directory to .txt files in an output directory.
Tries pdfminer first; falls back to pdfplumber for complex layouts.
Logs failures for manual follow-up.

Usage: python pdf_to_text.py <pdf_dir> <text_dir>
"""

import sys
import os
from pathlib import Path
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(levelname)s: %(message)s')
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def extract_with_pdfminer(pdf_path):
    from pdfminer.high_level import extract_text
    return extract_text(str(pdf_path))

def extract_with_pdfplumber(pdf_path):
    import pdfplumber
    text = []
    with pdfplumber.open(str(pdf_path)) as pdf:
        for page in pdf.pages:
            page_text = page.extract_text()
            if page_text:
                text.append(page_text)
    return "\n\n".join(text)

def convert_pdf(pdf_path, output_dir):
    stem = pdf_path.stem
    out_path = output_dir / f"{stem}.txt"
    
    if out_path.exists():
        log.info(f"Skipping {stem} (already converted)")
        return True

    try:
        text = extract_with_pdfminer(pdf_path)
        if len(text.strip()) < 100:
            raise ValueError("pdfminer returned minimal text — likely scanned PDF")
        out_path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        log.info(f"Converted: {stem}")
        return True
    except Exception as e1:
        log.warning(f"pdfminer failed for {stem}: {e1} — trying pdfplumber")
        try:
            text = extract_with_pdfplumber(pdf_path)
            if len(text.strip()) < 100:
                raise ValueError("pdfplumber also returned minimal text")
            out_path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
            log.info(f"Converted (pdfplumber): {stem}")
            return True
        except Exception as e2:
            log.error(f"FAILED: {stem} — {e2}")
            return False

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python pdf_to_text.py <pdf_dir> <text_dir>")
        sys.exit(1)

    pdf_dir = Path(sys.argv[1])
    text_dir = Path(sys.argv[2])
    text_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    pdfs = list(pdf_dir.glob("*.pdf"))
    if not pdfs:
        log.warning(f"No PDFs found in {pdf_dir}")
        sys.exit(0)

    log.info(f"Found {len(pdfs)} PDFs to convert")
    failed = []

    for pdf_path in sorted(pdfs):
        success = convert_pdf(pdf_path, text_dir)
        if not success:
            failed.append(pdf_path.name)

    log.info(f"\nDone. {len(pdfs) - len(failed)}/{len(pdfs)} converted successfully.")
    if failed:
        fail_log = text_dir / "conversion-failures.txt"
        fail_log.write_text("\n".join(failed))
        log.warning(f"{len(failed)} failures logged to {fail_log}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Install dependencies:**
```bash
pip install pdfminer.six pdfplumber
```

**Run:**
```bash
python tools/scripts/pdf_to_text.py [project]/data/pdfs/ [project]/data/texts/
```

**Output:** One `.txt` file per PDF in `[project]/data/texts/`. Failures logged to `conversion-failures.txt`.

> **Note for Paul:** If you have a script that handles OCR (scanned PDFs via pytesseract or similar), that would be a significant improvement over this version. The naming convention we need is: input filename preserved as output filename, `.pdf` → `.txt`, no other transformation.

---

## Stage 5 — Synthesis Pass

**Goal:** Generate a synthesis document from the full-text corpus. Discuss with the model.

1. Open a new Claude session (or Gemini if corpus size exceeds context).
2. Provide the model with:
   - Your research question (1–2 sentences)
   - The `sources-aaa.bib` file (for metadata context)
   - The contents of `[project]/data/texts/` (paste or reference)
3. Ask the model to generate a **synthesis document**: a thematic overview of what the corpus covers, where it agrees, where it tensions, what it leaves unresolved.
4. Discuss the synthesis with the model. This is not passive reading — push back, ask for clarification, redirect emphasis.
5. Save the synthesis as `[project]/data/synthesis-v1.md`.

---

## Stage 6 — Co-Author the Essay

**Goal:** Produce a working draft of the literature review through iterative model collaboration.

1. From the synthesis, identify 3–5 major themes or tensions that organize the literature.
2. Work theme by theme with the model: "Emphasize X. Downplay Y. Here is what I want to argue in this section."
3. The model drafts; you edit; you return the edited version to the model for the next section or pass.
4. The draft never leaves the model entirely — you are molding it together, not generating it in one shot.
5. Export a working draft to Google Docs or a markdown file for broader editing when ready.
6. **The sources you cite in the draft are your signal.** Note which sources you actually used — these drive Stage 7.

---

## Stage 7 — Extract Zettels

**Goal:** Distill the ideas that emerged from writing into atomic zettel notes.

1. After drafting, query the model: "Across the sources I cited, what are the recurring methods?" "What are the key findings?" "Where do the sources disagree?"
2. Each answer is a candidate zettel. The scholar reviews, refines, splits, or merges.
3. Write each zettel using the `//zet` skill format:
   - Title: the single idea (5 words max)
   - Body: dense synthesis (100 words max)
   - `sources:` YAML field: list of DOIs or handles that support this idea
4. Tag each zettel with `validation_status: unvalidated`.
5. Save to `people/[contributor]/aix-zettel/notes/`.

**Validation gates:**
- At **5+ sources** on a zettel: run a machine check — re-query the model: "Do all these sources genuinely support the claim in this zettel, or have I conflated distinct ideas?" If the model flags conflation, split the zettel.
- At **20+ sources** on a zettel: human validation required — read a representative sample yourself, write a synthesis argument, upgrade `validation_status` to `human-validated`. This zettel is now a finding.

---

## Stage 8 — Spiral

**Goal:** Extend the corpus based on what the draft revealed as important.

1. Take the sources you cited in Stage 6.
2. For each: collect (a) everything it cites, and (b) everything that cites it (use Google Scholar's "Cited by" feature or Semantic Scholar).
3. Add newly discovered sources to Zotero. Abstract-screen them. Tag promising ones `aaa`.
4. Re-run Stages 3–7 on the new batch.
5. Each spiral deepens the zettel graph and may revise earlier zettels.
6. Stop spiraling when new sources stop producing new zettel candidates — the graph has stabilized.

---

## File and Folder Conventions

```
[project]/
├── data/
│   ├── sources-aaa.bib          ← Zotero export, aaa-tagged sources only
│   ├── missing-pdfs.md          ← sources without PDFs, for manual follow-up
│   ├── pdfs/                    ← original PDF files
│   ├── texts/                   ← converted .txt files (one per PDF)
│   │   └── conversion-failures.txt
│   └── synthesis-v1.md          ← model-generated synthesis document
├── methods/
│   └── literature-review-workflow.md   ← this document
```

Zettel notes go to `people/[contributor]/aix-zettel/notes/` — not inside the project folder.

---

## Key Principles

- **The zettel is an idea, not a source.** One zettel, many sources. Never one source, one zettel.
- **DOI is the citation anchor.** Full metadata is fetched at citation time only.
- **The essay is a byproduct.** The zettel graph is the durable artifact. The essay is one run of one pipeline configuration.
- **Version the recipe.** Commit your synthesis prompts, validation thresholds, and extraction instructions alongside the corpus. Future runs are reproducible.
- **The model is a reading partner, not a summarizer.** What you bring to the conversation shapes what you get back.

    try:
        text = extract_with_pdfminer(pdf_path)
        if len(text.strip()) < 100:
            raise ValueError("pdfminer returned minimal text — likely scanned PDF")
        out_path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        log.info(f"Converted: {stem}")
        return True
    except Exception as e1:
        log.warning(f"pdfminer failed for {stem}: {e1} — trying pdfplumber")
        try:
            text = extract_with_pdfplumber(pdf_path)
            if len(text.strip()) < 100:
                raise ValueError("pdfplumber also returned minimal text")
            out_path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
            log.info(f"Converted (pdfplumber): {stem}")
            return True
        except Exception as e2:
            log.error(f"FAILED: {stem} — {e2}")
            return False

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        print("Usage: python pdf_to_text.py <pdf_dir> <text_dir>")
        sys.exit(1)

    pdf_dir = Path(sys.argv[1])
    text_dir = Path(sys.argv[2])
    text_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    pdfs = list(pdf_dir.glob("*.pdf"))
    if not pdfs:
        log.warning(f"No PDFs found in {pdf_dir}")
        sys.exit(0)

    log.info(f"Found {len(pdfs)} PDFs to convert")
    failed = []

    for pdf_path in sorted(pdfs):
        success = convert_pdf(pdf_path, text_dir)
        if not success:
            failed.append(pdf_path.name)

    log.info(f"\nDone. {len(pdfs) - len(failed)}/{len(pdfs)} converted successfully.")
    if failed:
        fail_log = text_dir / "conversion-failures.txt"
        fail_log.write_text("\n".join(failed))
        log.warning(f"{len(failed)} failures logged to {fail_log}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

---

## Stage 5 — Synthesis Pass

**Goal:** Generate a synthesis document from the full-text corpus. Discuss with the model.

1. Open a new Claude session (or Gemini if corpus size exceeds context).
2. Provide the model with:
   - Your research question (1–2 sentences)
   - The `sources-aaa.bib` file (for metadata context)
   - The contents of `[project]/data/texts/` (paste or reference)
3. Ask the model to generate a **synthesis document**: a thematic overview of what the corpus covers, where it agrees, where it tensions, what it leaves unresolved.
4. Discuss the synthesis with the model. This is not passive reading — push back, ask for clarification, redirect emphasis.
5. Save the synthesis as `[project]/data/synthesis-v1.md`.

---

## Stage 6 — Co-Author the Essay

**Goal:** Produce a working draft of the literature review through iterative model collaboration.

1. From the synthesis, identify 3–5 major themes or tensions that organize the literature.
2. Work theme by theme with the model: "Emphasize X. Downplay Y. Here is what I want to argue in this section."
3. The model drafts; you edit; you return the edited version to the model for the next section or pass.
4. The draft never leaves the model entirely — you are molding it together, not generating it in one shot.
5. Export a working draft to Google Docs or a markdown file for broader editing when ready.
6. **The sources you cite in the draft are your signal.** Note which sources you actually used — these drive Stage 7.

---

## Stage 7 — Extract Zettels

**Goal:** Distill the ideas that emerged from writing into atomic zettel notes.

1. After drafting, query the model: "Across the sources I cited, what are the recurring methods?" "What are the key findings?" "Where do the sources disagree?"
2. Each answer is a candidate zettel. The scholar reviews, refines, splits, or merges.
3. Write each zettel using the `//zet` skill format:
   - Title: the single idea (5 words max)
   - Body: dense synthesis (100 words max)
   - `sources:` YAML field: list of DOIs or handles that support this idea
4. Tag each zettel with `validation_status: unvalidated`.
5. Save to `people/[contributor]/aix-zettel/notes/`.

**Validation gates:**
- At **5+ sources** on a zettel: run a machine check — re-query the model: "Do all these sources genuinely support the claim in this zettel, or have I conflated distinct ideas?" If the model flags conflation, split the zettel.
- At **20+ sources** on a zettel: human validation required — read a representative sample yourself, write a synthesis argument, upgrade `validation_status` to `human-validated`. This zettel is now a finding.

---

## Stage 8 — Spiral

**Goal:** Extend the corpus based on what the draft revealed as important.

1. Take the sources you cited in Stage 6.
2. For each: collect (a) everything it cites, and (b) everything that cites it (use Google Scholar's "Cited by" feature or Semantic Scholar).
3. Add newly discovered sources to Zotero. Abstract-screen them. Tag promising ones `aaa`.
4. Re-run Stages 3–7 on the new batch.
5. Each spiral deepens the zettel graph and may revise earlier zettels.
6. Stop spiraling when new sources stop producing new zettel candidates — the graph has stabilized.

---

## File and Folder Conventions

```
[project]/
├── data/
│   ├── sources-aaa.bib          ← Zotero export, aaa-tagged sources only
│   ├── missing-pdfs.md          ← sources without PDFs, for manual follow-up
│   ├── pdfs/                    ← original PDF files
│   ├── texts/                   ← converted .txt files (one per PDF)
│   │   └── conversion-failures.txt
│   └── synthesis-v1.md          ← model-generated synthesis document
├── methods/
│   └── literature-review-workflow.md   ← this document
```

Zettel notes go to `people/[contributor]/aix-zettel/notes/` — not inside the project folder.

---

## Key Principles

- **The zettel is an idea, not a source.** One zettel, many sources. Never one source, one zettel.
- **DOI is the citation anchor.** Full metadata is fetched at citation time only.
- **The essay is a byproduct.** The zettel graph is the durable artifact. The essay is one run of one pipeline configuration.
- **Version the recipe.** Commit your synthesis prompts, validation thresholds, and extraction instructions alongside the corpus. Future runs are reproducible.
- **The model is a reading partner, not a summarizer.** What you bring to the conversation shapes what you get back.

Instead of trying to comprehend it alone, you upload it, feed it into a large language model, and use the model as an interpretive partner. You formulate questions that help the model understand what you need to interpret. You work iteratively with the model's responses, deepening your comprehension. You evaluate when the model's interpretation helps and when your own expertise must prevail. Through this cycle of uploading, questioning, and integrating, you understand something complex with the model's help.
Writing with a Large Language Model: You have knowledge developed through your reasoning or analysis that you want to extend, articulate, and share with others. Rather than working alone, you write that thinking as prompts to a large language model—not polished or final, but genuine attempts to articulate what you're working through. The model generates responses. You read those responses, review them, and integrate them into your thinking—or use them as your thinking. You write more prompts based on what emerges. Through this cycle of writing, reading generated responses, and integrating them, your thinking becomes clearer and more precise. You generate texts, charts, or graphs that reflect your knowledge in a way you can share with others.
Both practices require skill, judgment, and intention. Both are different from simply requesting outputs and consuming them. Both are grounded in your expertise and your professional judgment.
